title: Repeated Validation inside an Already-Trusted Boundary
pattern: Internal helpers repeat range, null, or other invariant checks already established by an entry boundary or constructor and preserved on every reachable path, regardless of whether the inputs have already been validated by the calling boundary.
why_bad: Repeated defensive branches obscure which routine owns the invariant and duplicate validation logic without adding protection. Defensive code is just as prone to bugs as business code; scattered checks make the codebase fat and slow, bury the primary business logic, and signal that developers do not trust their own type system or class boundaries.
detection: The same condition is checked through internal layers even though validated types, constructor enforcement, and controlled mutation guarantee it at each use. Subcases: (a) extensive chains of simple parameter range, null, and boundary checks repeating across multiple layered internal function calls; (b) validation conditions inside private or internal methods checking invariants already strictly enforced by the public constructor or boundary method. Do not infer that a value is trusted solely because a function is private; the invariant must actually hold on every path reaching it.
fix: Designate strict "barricade" boundaries (entry points, constructors) where data is sanitized once, preserve the invariants through mutation, and remove genuinely redundant internal checks so the constructor or boundary validation is the sole source of truth. Internal routines may use diagnostic assertions where helpful without treating them as ingress validation.
source: Steve McConnell, *Code Complete*, Section 8.8 ("Being Defensive About Defensive Programming") and Section 8.5 ("Barricade Your Program"); Steve McConnell, *Code Complete*, Section 8.5 ("Relationship Between Barricades and Assertions").
